did_you_know.text: Did you know? The vineyard song begins with a description of a vineyard that was planted and carefully tended: its owner dug around it, cleared it of stones, planted it with a choice vine, built a tower, and hewed out a winepress—yet the vineyard produced wild grapes.

Did you know? The owner of the vineyard invites the residents of Jerusalem and the men of Judah to judge between him and his vineyard, leading them to decide for themselves whether everything possible had been done for the vineyard.

Did you know? Only at the end of the song is it revealed that the vineyard is the house of Israel and the men of Judah. The LORD hoped for justice and righteousness, but found “bloodshed” and “a cry of distress”—a wordplay emphasizing the gap between expectation and result.

Did you know? The prophet rebukes those who join house to house and field to field until no room remains for others. The sin described is not merely the accumulation of property, but an occupation that creates a society in which others are pushed off the land.

Did you know? The chapter uses agricultural units of measurement to describe the punishment of desolation: ten yoke of vineyard will yield only one bath, and a homer of seed will yield only one ephah.

Did you know? The feasts in the chapter include the lyre, harp, tambourine, flute, and wine, but the central problem is that the revelers do not pay attention to the LORD’s work or see what his hands have done.
Did you know? Sheol is portrayed vividly as enlarging its appetite and opening its mouth without limit; the image expresses the depth of the disaster and the multitude of those descending into it.

Did you know? The expression “those who draw iniquity with cords of falsehood” describes people who initially pull sin toward themselves with thin, worthless cords, and later “with ropes like those of a cart”—thicker and stronger ropes.
Did you know? One of the chapter’s rebukes is a deliberate moral reversal: people call evil good and good evil, and exchange darkness for light and bitter for sweet.

Did you know? After describing the people’s sins and punishment, the LORD raises a banner for distant nations and summons them to come. The enemy army is portrayed as a swift, disciplined, and armed force that arrives with a roar and brings darkness and distress.
